title: A Simple Way To Improve Listening
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin offers a step-by-step strategy for teaching students to follow directions the first time they're given, ending the exhausting cycle of cajoling and repeating instructions. The method involves standing in one spot, giving directions only once in a normal voice, then remaining motionless while students figure it out on their own, even if they initially struggle. Class leaders will naturally emerge to help others, and over repeated practice directions get followed faster and with fewer prompts. He recommends starting with simple, low-stakes directions to build the habit before increasing complexity. The underlying principle is that students only tune out because they know a teacher will repeat themselves; removing that safety net makes them learn to listen the first time.
points: Give directions from a fixed spot in the room, spoken once in a normal voice, rather than repeating or cajoling.
Remain motionless and silent after giving directions, letting students struggle and self-organize rather than jumping in to help.
Class leaders will naturally emerge to model or repeat directions for peers, which should be allowed to happen.
Start with simple, low-stakes directions to build the habit before increasing complexity over time.
Students become poor listeners specifically because they know a teacher will repeat instructions; removing that expectation restores attentive listening.
quotes: But the solution isn’t so difficult. In fact, with just a few simple steps you can teach your students to listen and follow your directions the first—and only—time they’re given.
After receiving their quiet attention, give the directions you want them to follow one time—which is the key the strategy.
Resist the urge to jump in and repeat yourself, cajole, or talk them through what you want them to do. Just stand in place and observe.
Slowly, leaders will emerge to either model for the others what to do or speak up and do the cajoling and repeating for you.
Students become poor listeners when they know they don’t have to listen.
When they know you’ll repeat yourself and hold their hand through every direction and every lesson, they have no reason to listen.
